title: Perineuronal nets in the bed nucleus of stria terminalis mediate stress-induced anxiety behaviour in adult male mice
authors: Murrall, K.; Mucha, M.; Mujmer, K.; Ten Blanco, M.; Sherlock, B.; Pawlak, R.; Mosienko, V.
abstract: Anxiety disorders affect an estimated 301.4 million people globally. However, they remain among the most challenging conditions to treat, with only around half of patients reporting a 50% or greater reduction in their symptoms. The discovery of novel and more effective treatments therefore requires a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms of anxiety at both the circuit and cellular levels. Stress induces aberrant changes in neuronal plasticity across brain regions within the anxiety circuitry including the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST). One mechanism through which synaptic plasticity is regulated is the organisation of perineuronal nets (PNNs), specialised extracellular matrix structures that are highly sensitive to stress. In rodent models, stress is associated with a reduction in PNN number and/or decreased Wisteria floribunda Agglutinin (WFA) labelling in limbic areas. However, the development of PNNs within the BNST and their role in the stress responsiveness remain largely unknown. In the current study we investigated the spatiotemporal development of PNNs within the BNST of male mice, where they first appear at P30 and continue to mature into adulthood, reaching their highest expression at P210 and specifically within the anteromedial BNST. We further showed that stress-induced anxiety is associated with a reduction in PNN number and significant changes to PNN fine structure including increased leakiness in the anteromedial BNST. Most importantly, enzymatic removal of PNNs by chondroitinase ABC in the mouse anteromedial BNST exacerbated behavioural responses to acute stress as demonstrated by increased anxiety-like behaviour. Collectively, these results highlight an indispensable role for PNNs within the anteromedial BNST in mediating a healthy emotional response to psychosocial stress.

title: Fast Generalized Longitudinal Functional Principal Components Analysis with Applications to Population-Level Neuronal Dynamics
authors: Duffy, K. A.; Pai, N.; Schneck, D.; Kozienko, G.; Zheng, L.; Xenopoulos-Oddsson, A.; Wang, J.; Johnson, L. A.; Vitek, J.; Fiecas, M.; Cui, E.
abstract: Functional data are widely collected across many fields. One approach for modeling functional data collected across repeated measures is longitudinal functional PCA (LFPCA), which allows for the decomposition of variability at multiple levels. However, existing estimation approaches for LFPCA can be computationally demanding for large or high-dimensional datasets. Here, we propose fast generalized LFPCA, a novel estimation technique that bins data along the functional domain and fits a marginal mixed model at each bin. Simulation results show that the proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than existing techniques while achieving similar accuracy, making LFPCA scalable to datasets with more densely sampled observations and larger sample sizes. We apply the proposed technique to model neuronal firing rate data both on and off deep brain stimulation (DBS) to investigate how the intervention modulates population-level neuronal activity. Our results suggest that the vast majority of between-neuron variation can be explained by four principal components, which relate to individual differences in neuronal firing as well as the arm manipulation paradigm under study. We also find that DBS significantly increases the variability of firing activity, likely driven by increased firing from a subset of neurons in response to DBS, a novel insight not obtained in previous analyses. Code to implement the proposed method and run simulation studies is included in the supplement.

title: Determining cellular phylogeny and migration at high resolution in spatial genomics
authors: Zhang, D.; Jiang, Y.; Yu, X.; Bai, D.; Tian, J.; Enninful, A.; Tian, X.; Li, H.; Huo, Y.; Chen, Y.; Yao, N.; Li, J.; Chu, Z.; Bai, Z.; Fan, R.; Lu, J.; Gerstein, M.
abstract: Cellular migration and tumor evolution are central to tissue homeostasis and cancer biology. Rapid advances in spatial genomics have raised the possibility of using somatic mutations to track these processes in situ in human tissues. However, frequent data dropouts in spatial genomics measurements make this challenging to implement. Here, we present StarTrak (SpaTial Analysis for lineage ReconsTRuction with somatic vAriant calling and tracKing), a framework for somatic variant calling and lineage reconstruction at single-pixel spatial resolution. StarTrak employs a neural network framework to integrate mutational evidence (from both nuclear and mitochondrial reads), spatial proximity, histological images, and transcriptomic states to identify spatially informative patterns of mutations. It performs robustly across tissue types and spatial-omics platforms (being particularly successful with spatial ATAC-seq). Applying StarTrak to tumor sections, we infer the migration of mutated tumor cells into adjacent non-malignant tissues and reconstruct distinct lineage trees associated with different spatial regions. Notably, we identify tumor regions with nearly identical transcriptomic states but distinct mutational profiles. Moreover, for skin sections, StarTrak identifies sunlight-associated mutations in non-malignant epidermis and evidence suggesting the migration of these mutant surface cells into deeper skin layers. Overall, by integrating mutation calling with spatial context, StarTrak enables the inference of spatially resolved cellular migration and cellular phylogeny.

title: Longitudinal associations between task-control network functioning, cognition, and the environment in early adolescence
authors: Paige, K. J.; Michael, C.; Molloy, M. F.; Kardan, O.; Angstadt, M.; Sripada, C.; Hyde, L.; Heitzeg, M.; Weigard, A.
abstract: Neural maturation in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks is thought to support the development of adolescents' cognitive and adaptive functioning. Further, theory suggests that family and neighborhood contexts shape brain network development. Yet, few longitudinal studies have examined the co-development of brain network mechanisms with cognitive and adaptive functioning or with environmental factors that could shape the maturation of these mechanisms. The present study addressed these gaps. We used longitudinal data spanning late childhood (Mage=10 years) to early adolescence (Mage=12) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (n=4862). Stable and construct-valid neural signatures of task-control network functioning were estimated using longitudinal bifactor modeling of neural responses to cognitive demand during the n-back task. Multivariate latent change-score models were used to examine co-development of this signature with cognitive efficiency (drift rate from the diffusion model), teacher-reported attention problems, family conflict, and neighborhood safety. Models accounted for baseline family income. Robust reciprocal relations between task-control activation and cognitive efficiency were identified and the latent change scores for efficiency and task-control activation were positively correlated. Similar reciprocal associations were observed between cognitive efficiency and attention problems. Baseline family income predicted the rate of change in task-control network functioning. This study demonstrates that task-control network functioning co-develops with cognition, which in turn supports attentional functioning development across early adolescence. Further, findings highlight the utility of this neural signature of task-control network functioning for understanding the neural basis of cognitive development and the mechanisms through which environmental experiences shape brain and behavior.

title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
authors: Philippe, V.; Tombroff, L.; Akbarian, F.; De Witte, S.; Trotta, N.; Van Schependom, J.; Engelborghs, S.; Bier, J.-C.; Strauss, M.; De Tiege, X.; Wens, V.
abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

title: An anatomy-constrained transcriptomic screen identifies a 19-gene panel with an ordered regional similarity pattern in the human somatosensory system
authors: Boni, G. A.; Luque Hernandez, A.; Bautista Ruedas, V. I.
abstract: Neuroanatomical pathways link specialized brain regions, but whether regional transcriptomic profiles preserve relationships aligned with pathway order remains unclear. We defined candidate pathways and their available tissue representations from neuroanatomical literature, then screened 10,262 genes in the Body Index of Gene Expression (BIGE), a human microarray resource covering cells and tissues. The screen required expression across every mapped region of a route and limited single-region dominance. It identified 23 candidates in three routes with sufficient coverage; 19 met the criteria for the dorsal column-medial lemniscus (DCML) representation and formed the fixed panel. We evaluated this panel in six Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) donors across three central regional representations: an aggregate of samples assigned to the cuneate and gracile nuclei (Cu/Gr), the lateral group of nuclei, ventral division, within the dorsal thalamus (DTLv), and postcentral gyrus. The regional-order contrast compared the mean similarity of the pairs adjacent in the anatomical sequence, Cu/Gr-DTLv and DTLv-postcentral gyrus, with Cu/Gr-postcentral gyrus similarity. Both adjacent-in-order correlations were positive in all six donors; the contrast was positive in five and reached a mean of T = 0.345175 (exact sign test, P = 0.109375). The panel exceeded two distributions of 50,000 gene sets generated under comparable selection constraints (P = 0.027919 and P = 0.026579). In descriptive anatomical comparisons, it ranked third among 240 combinations and first among the target and all 16 single-region substitutions. All 50,000 one-probe-per-gene analyses retained T > 0, and broad neuronal-expression contrasts were positive in medulla, thalamus, and cortex. Spatial support depended on the null model, with stronger evidence under whole-donor surrogates (P = 0.003860) than under the primary within-compartment model (P = 0.051179). These findings identify a fixed gene panel whose regional similarity is aligned with the represented central order of the DCML system and define a specific hypothesis for prospective evaluation in an independent, anatomically resolved dataset.

title: Sample overlap in genome-wide association meta-analysis: practical comparisons across significance thresholds
authors: Xu, Z.; Zhang, L.; Elliott, L. T.
abstract: Meta-analysis is widely used in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to combine evidence across studies without requiring individual-level data. However, as both the number of studies included in meta-analyses and their sample sizes continue to grow, the same participant may be included in more than one study. Such sample overlap induces dependence across studies and violates the independence assumptions underlying standard meta-analysis methods. HostSeq is a Canadian initiative in which 15 clinical and epidemiological studies were assembled with DNA samples from approximately 10,000 Canadians infected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. We observed duplicate samples across different participating studies. This observation raises an important practical question: what is the impact of sample overlap on association results, and when should such overlap be a concern? Motivated by this real problem, we sought to compare five meta-analysis methods and evaluate their performance against a reference mega-analysis in which the true sample overlap is known. We show that when the degree of sample overlap is relatively small, its impact on association results is minimal, even at the genome-wide significance threshold of = 5*10 -8 . We demonstrate these findings through extensive simulation studies and an application to overlapping cohorts within HostSeq.

title: Scalable Enzyme Reaction Retrieval Enables Metagenomic Biocatalyst Discovery
authors: Luo, D.; Jiang, M.; Wang, B.
abstract: Enzyme catalyzed reactions drive metabolism and enable diverse applications in biotechnology and sustainable synthesis, but assigning catalytic functions to uncharacterized enzymes and finding enzymes for target reactions remain major challenges. Despite recent advances in machine learning, translating enzyme function prediction into systematic discovery across the vast space of uncharacterized proteins and biochemical reactions remains challenging. Here we present EzHit, a lightweight framework for bidirectional enzyme reaction retrieval. Across enzyme annotation, orphan-reaction retrieval and family-specific fine-tuning benchmarks, EzHit achieved strong top-ranked performance and outperformed representative enzyme reaction matching baselines. We further show that Mahalanobis distance based geometric confidence provides more useful reliability estimates than probability-derived uncertainty metrics or evidential learning, enabling confidence-aware prioritization of high scoring candidates. Owing to its efficiency, EzHit was applied to a nearly trillion-scale OMG_Prot50 with RHEA screen, yielding 8.20 billion retained enzyme reaction associations across 30.27 million predicted enzyme sequences. Experimental validation further confirmed the activity of EzHit prioritized metagenomic enzyme candidates for a sparsely annotated reaction. Together, these results establish EzHit as a scalable framework for enzyme annotation, reaction-guided mining and biocatalyst discovery

title: Action-related brain dynamics during leader-follower coordination
authors: Ruuskanen, S.; Avendano-Diaz, J. C.; Hari, R.; Parkkonen, L.
abstract: Leader-follower dynamics are essential for social interaction, enabling smooth inter-personal coordination. Although neuroimaging studies have identified brain networks associated with leading and following, the dynamical brain signatures supporting these roles remain poorly characterized. Here, sixteen dyads performed a joint-improvisation mirror-game task with predefined leader-follower roles while magnetoencephalography (MEG) and hand kinematics (acceleration) were simultaneously recorded. We investigated role-specific modulations of source-space MEG activity in delta (0.54 Hz), theta (4-8 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), and gamma (40-90 Hz) frequency bands, as well as coherence between cortical activity and movement kinematics. Compared with leaders, followers exhibited stronger theta-band activity in a cluster comprising frontal, cingulate, and sensorimotor regions, and stronger coherence between movement kinematics and occipital cortical activity, consistent with enhanced monitoring, adaptation, and reliance on visual kinematic information. In contrast, leaders showed reduced alpha-band power in sensorimotor and premotor regions, and stronger beta-band activity in occipital cortices, likely reflecting greater demands for action planning and predictive control. Our results identify complementary spectral and action-related brain signatures associated with leader-follower coordination during joint improvisation, providing new insights into the neural underpinnings of real-time interpersonal coordination.

title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
authors: Yenikapati, M. S.; Deshpande, S.; Desai, S. P.; Santine, D. D.; Roghani, A. K.
abstract: Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human. Keywords: Speech neuroprosthesis, paralinguistics, BCI, naturalistic communication

title: Pilifers provide rapid mechanosensory feedback during floral tracking in hawkmoths
authors: Anand, M.; Torres, M.; Brunton, B. W.; Daniel, T. L.; Weber, A. I.; Deora, T.
abstract: Hawkmoths expertly hover over flowers during feeding, accurately tracking floral movements even as flowers gently sway in the wind. They use visual and mechanosensory feedback to adjust their position, while their long, flexible mouthpart, the proboscis, stays inserted inside the nectar spur. Although much is known about how hawkmoths detect and process visual motion, far less is understood about how hawkmoths detect mechanical motion cues. Pilifers are hair bundles at the proboscis-head joint, well-positioned to provide feedback about floral motion. Here, we tested if pilifers could provide mechanosensory feedback essential for successful floral tracking. We computed bending at the proboscis base during floral tracking in freely flying hawkmoths and found that floral movements induce small yet significantly correlated lateral bending. Recordings from pilifer afferents showed that they respond to lateral motions of amplitudes similar to those seen in natural floral tracking behaviors. They respond to different directions and speeds of proboscis motion with an average latency of 1.9 ms. Neural tracing revealed extensive sensory arborizations in the sub-esophageal ganglion of the brain and ventral nerve cord, indicating a feedback pathway to the neck and flight motor system that enables rapid coordination of appendages and body for successful feeding.

title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
authors: Carreno Munoz, M. I.; Chehrazi, P.; Ciancone Chama, A.; Knoth, I.; Fernandes do Nascimento, S. A.; Campbell, B.; Csicsvari, J.; Chattopadhyaya, B.; Lippe, S.; Di Cristo, G.
abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
authors: Nuttin, B.; Sans-Dublanc, A.; Chrzanowska, A.; Liu, C.; Hanson, L.; Drakaki, Z.; Luyks, R.; Bruystreen, A.; Philipon, A.; Grillet, M.; Kuhn, N.; Goncalves, P.; Montaldo, G.; Bonin, V.; Urban, A.; Farrow, K.
abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

title: Exposure to childhood adversity and adult alcohol, nicotine, and illicit drug use in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis of the German National Cohort (NAKO)
authors: Boehmer, J.; Meyer-Degering, K.; Ghadami, A.; Sreepada, A.; Bohmann, P.; Castell, S.; Feuchtinger, M.; Gottschick, C.; Grabe, H. J.; Karch, A.; Lahmann, C.; Lang, A.; Leitzmann, M.; Meinke-Franze, C.; Meyerdierks, D.; Mikolajczyk, R.; Nimptsch, K.; Obi, N.; Peters, A.; Pischon, T.; Stein, M. J.; Keil, T.; Krist, L.; Tost, H.; Heim, C. C.
abstract: Rationale: Exposure to adversity in childhood and adolescence (i.e., "early-life stress"; ELS) is a well-established risk factor for substance use. Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate associations between ELS exposure and substance use across subtypes of ELS, different substance classes, and behavioral profiles of substance use. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we examined associations between ELS exposure and substance use in a population-based sample of 172,173 adults aged 19-74 years from the German National Cohort (NAKO). ELS exposure was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Screener. Substance use included nicotine, alcohol, and illicit drug use. Associations were examined using regression models evaluating overall ELS exposure, cumulative trauma load, and ELS subtypes. Latent class analysis (LCA) was conducted to identify substance use profiles. Results: ELS exposure was associated with higher odds of smoking, greater smoking severity, heavier alcohol consumption among drinkers, and higher odds of lifetime illicit drug use. Overall, the strongest associations were observed for opioid and stimulant use. Dose-response analyses revealed higher risk with increasing numbers of ELS subtypes. Abuse-related subtypes, particularly exposure to physical and sexual abuse, consistently showed strongest independent associations across substances, whereas neglect exhibited weaker, more variable associations. LCA identified four substance use profiles, with ELS exposure predicting membership in more severe polysubstance classes. Conclusions: ELS emerged as a robust risk factor for adult substance use, underscoring the need for trauma-informed approaches in clinical practice, public health, and policy to mitigate the long-term consequences of early adversity.

title: LIF is a pro-algesic mediator in human and mouse models of arthritis-related pain
authors: Ross, R.; Li, Y.; Vlachaki Walker, J.; Ali Awadelkareem, M.; Zebochin, I.; Goodwin, G. L.; Marin, A.-C.; Trendafilova, T.; Montague, I.; Rutter-Locher, Z.; Ryan, S.; Baldeweg, F.; Freytag, K.; Condor, R.; Arridge, N.; Buckley, C. D.; Bennett, D.; Humby, F.; Kirkham, B.; Denk, F.; Taams, L.
abstract: Purpose: Emerging clinical and experimental data suggest that JAK inhibitors (JAKi) are effective in reducing pain in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). We recently showed that JAK/STAT signalling cytokines, specifically IL-6, LIF and IL-11, are present in the RA joint and can act directly on human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived sensory neurons by increasing their STAT3 phosphorylation (pSTAT3) levels and expression of select pain-relevant genes. In this study, we determined that LIF is the most consequential cytokine out of the three, altering neuronal signalling, outgrowth and pain-like behaviours in in vitro and in vivo models of arthritis. Methods: Human iPSC-derived sensory neurons were stimulated with RA synovial fluid (SF) or with cytokine-treated RA synovial fibroblast conditioned media (CM) in the absence or presence of anti-cytokine antibodies. pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels, and gene expression patterns, were assessed by Western blot and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq). The immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6) was assessed for LIF-induced JAK/STAT signalling in addition to neurite outgrowth assays as a functional readout of the sensory neurons. Lastly, mouse models were used to assess pain-related behaviours in vivo. Results: LIF was found to be consistently present in the SF from painful joints from individuals with inflammatory arthritis. Western blotting revealed that the addition of RA SF to iPSC-derived sensory neurons led to LIF-dependent induction of pSTAT3 and pSTAT1, while RNA-seq demonstrated that LIF alters the transcriptome of sensory neurons more prominently than IL-6 and IL-11, up-regulating signature genes related to peripheral neuron sensitization, such as TRPV1, NTRK1, BDNF, HRH1 and SCN10A. Similarly, cytokine-treated fibroblast conditioned media was shown to induce neuronal pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 and upregulate expression of BDNF, HRH1 and VGF in a LIF-dependent manner. Additionally, the immortalised dorsal root ganglion (DRG)-derived cell line (HD 10.6), which also exhibited LIF-induced pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, showed increased neurite outgrowth after axotomy when treated with LIF. Finally, in a mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, LIF was shown to be significantly increased in the affected joint. Furthermore, intraarticular injection of LIF into a healthy mouse knee resulted in increased responsiveness to painful pressure stimuli in that joint. Conclusions: Our data indicate that LIF may be a pro-algesic mediator and a possible therapeutic target to improve pain management in individuals living with inflammatory arthritis.

title: Real-Time Neurotransmitter Sensing in Midbrain Organoids Using 3D Carbon Cup Electrodes
authors: Tavares da Silva Maraschin, S.; Thongkorn, S.; Kanakkottu, S.; Rezaei, B.; Scordo, G.; Sozzi, E.; Parmar, M.; Heiskanen, A.; Keller, S. S.; Emneus, J.
abstract: Real time, chemically selective detection of neurotransmitter release in brain organoids remains a challenge due to their complex three dimensional architecture and limited optical accessibility. We introduce 3D printed carbon cup electrodes (CCEs) -pyrolyzed, multi level pillar structures - designed to confine a single organoid, increase electroactive surface area, and enable amperometric recordings of oxidizable neurotransmitters. The CCEs exhibit excellent electrochemical performance and reproducibility, supporting diffusion controlled dopamine redox behavior without interference from culture medium. Using ventral midbrain (vMB) organoids at two maturation stages (Day 30 and Day 90), we demonstrate real time detection of potassium evoked dopamine release directly from organoids. Mature organoids exhibit higher peak currents, correlating with increased tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression confirmed by immunocytochemistry. Embedding organoids in Matrigel significantly attenuates dopamine signals, indicating a diffusion barrier that limits stimulant access and/or dopamine transport to the electrode. Repetitive stimulations reveal progressive depletion of dopamine stores, consistent with diminished vesicular release. Chemical perturbations using 6 hydroxydopamine and verapamil further validate the platform by producing substantial reductions in dopamine release accompanied by loss of TH neurons. These results establish CCEs as a powerful tool for label free, real-time monitoring of neurotransmission in human organoids, with potential for multiplexed sensing and integration of enzymatic detection strategies for non electroactive neurotransmitters.

title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
authors: Lan, Z.; Onoe, H.; Tsukiyama, T.; Iwatani, C.; Chen, C.-Y.; Okita, K.; Ishizuka, K.; Endo, R.; Nakai, R.; Imamura, K.; Hikishima, K.; Tsuchiya, H.; Nakaya, M.; Fang, Y.; Kobayashi, A.; Shinto, Y.; Yamaguchi, R.; Matsunaga, M.; Oe, K.; Omori, K.; Ozeki, Y.; Tomoda, T.; Miura, K.; Urayama, S.-i.; Oishi, N.; Okada, T.; Tanaka, M.; Inoue, H.; Takahashi, J.; Sawa, A.; Isa, T.
abstract: Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
authors: Kubo, Y.; Delanois, E.; Bazhenov, M.
abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory, which had taken over the inputs of older memories during new learning. The excitation/inhibition balance of inputs onto this population shifted toward inhibition, most strongly from older-memory populations, so that older memories again activated their own neurons. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: synaptic weights onto the reactivated population decrease when its neurons fire while their presynaptic partners are silent. The mechanism held under a synapse-level Dale's law, and excitatory plasticity alone, with inhibitory synapses fixed, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation.

title: Targeting skin ageing at the source: a novel cellular reprogramming approach using natural extract combinations
authors: Perciato, M. L.; Davies, M.; Akhbari, P.; Denise, H.; Clauss, A.; Cole, S. L.; Haas, K. M.; Lee, B.; Jouy, C.; Ballihaut, C.; Lee, B. P.; Harries, L. W.
abstract: Cellular senescence is a driver of skin ageing that leads to structural deterioration and aesthetic changes. This study evaluated a novel senomorphic strategy, using synergistic combinations of natural small molecules to target RNA splicing regulation via upstream ERK/AKT signaling pathways. Nature-identical synthetic molecules, and corresponding extracts were assessed for cytotoxicity, impact on senescent cell load, proliferation, DNA damage load and SASP markers in naturally aged human primary skin cells. A topical, simple formulation was evaluated for impact on senescence and skin structure using 3D human ex vivo full-thickness skin explants exposed to 1.5 J/cm2 UVC irradiation. Combination of H. lupulus and G. biloba extracts produced a dose-dependent senomorphic impact of up to 45% in aged dermal fibroblasts and 10% in aged human primary keratinocytes (p [≤] 0.0001 & 0.001), without inducing cell proliferation. A 50% decrease in DNA damage load was also observed (p [≤] 0.0001). Qualitatively, the simple formulation mitigated UV-induced epidermal hyperplasia, restored collagen fiber organization, and reduced markers of senescence and inflammation. Targeting cellular senescence is an emerging traction point to address the root biological causes of skin ageing. Targeting the splicing dysregulation/senescence axis using combinations of natural plant extracts may provide a novel mode of action to reprogram senescent cells for repair and protection of skin structure and function.

title: N-terminal truncation diversifies USP18 function during early myogenesis
authors: Raz, V.; Nijssen, T.; Draganov, S.; Shademan, M.; Vendrell, I.; Kessler, B. M.; Pinto-Fernandez, A.; flannery, S.
abstract: Ubiquitin-specific protease 18 (USP18) is primarily studied for its dual role in type-I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. At basal levels, however, USP18 also regulates muscle cell development, independently of IFN-I signaling. USP18 exists as a canonical long isoform (LF) and a short isoform (SF) generated by N-terminal truncation. Endogenous SF accumulates in the nucleus during muscle differentiation, but its cellular functions remain poorly understood. Here, we compared USP18 SF and LF in muscle cells stably overexpressing each isoform. We show that their distinct N-termini are associated with marked differences in protein stability, subcellular localization, and protein-protein interactions. SF displayed a substantially expanded interactome, with increased association with nuclear proteins, chaperones, and regulators of protein homeostasis. Functionally, SF enhanced an early stage of myogenic differentiation and was associated with changes in alternative splicing, including key sarcomere genes. Together, these findings identify the SF USP18 proteoform as a potential regulator of muscle differentiation and highlight the N-terminus as a determinant of non-canonical USP18 functions and proteoform diversity.

title: RiboGRAM learns multi-scale non-coding RNA grammar for structural and regulatory inference
authors: Wang, H.; Chen, Z.; Huang, H.; Li, S.; Jäschke, A.; Ye, Q.; Zhang, Y.
abstract: Protein-coding sequences are read through the triplet genetic code, whereas the organization of molecular information within non-coding RNA sequences remains elusive. Here, we identify a non-coding RNA grammar defined by multi-scale motif usage and 5'-to-3' positional gradients, and develop RiboGRAM to learn this organization. Across nine organisms, non-coding RNAs showed scale-dependent divergence from coding sequences, with directional U-rich and AU-rich gradients. Integrating multi-scale sequence encoding with contextual modeling, RiboGRAM organized RNA families, revealing motif-associated and pair-like patterns across layers. Without structural supervision, non-coding RNA pretraining improved base-pair recovery over coding or messenger RNA pretraining, with representations supporting alignment-free diffusion-based 3D modeling of short RNAs. In human RNA-protein binding profiles, RiboGRAM identified position-resolved motif organization across protein targets and cell types, with sequence-preference shifts associated with reduced cross-cell transferability. Together, these results establish a learnable grammar of non-coding RNA sequence organization for structural and regulatory inference.

title: Pan-cancer nucleosome landscapes reveal tumor heterogeneity and inform cell-free DNA-based detection
authors: Yang, S.; Ye, J.; Yuan, J.; Huang, X.; Yin, Y.; Liu, Z.; Li, W.; Li, Y.
abstract: Background: Nucleosome positioning and occupancy are fundamental features of chromatin organization, yet their variation across human cancers and potential utility for noninvasive cancer detection remain poorly characterized. Methods: We systematically characterized nucleosome organization across 410 primary tumors spanning 23 cancer types using ATAC-seq, establishing a high-confidence pan-cancer nucleosome atlas validated by independent MNase-seq data. We characterized shared and cancer-type-enriched nucleosome patterns, investigated their associations with tumor heterogeneity and regulatory alterations, and evaluated tissue-derived nucleosome signatures for cancer classification and detection using circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA). Results: The atlas identified shared and cancer-type-enriched nucleosomes associated with distinct regulatory programs. Notably, nucleosome occupancy provided information complementary to chromatin accessibility for tumor stratification and revealed molecular heterogeneity within individual cancers, including subgroups associated with Basal-like breast cancer. In hepatocellular carcinoma, differential nucleosome analysis revealed cancer-associated chromatin remodeling involving regulatory pathways, transcription factor motifs, and candidate genes. Importantly, tissue-derived nucleosome signatures were detectable in cfDNA, enabling classification among three cancer types (AUROC = 0.877) and colorectal cancer detection (AUROC = 0.930), with an AUROC of 0.773 in an independent validation cohort. We also developed OncoNucAtlas, a publicly accessible database facilitating exploration of these nucleosome landscapes. Conclusions: Our study cancer-associated nucleosome organization as a complementary source of epigenomic information and demonstrates the potential of tissue-derived nucleosome signatures for cfDNA-based cancer detection. The pan-cancer atlas provides a resource for investigating tumor heterogeneity and developing noninvasive cancer detection approaches.

title: PlasmoRhythm: A comprehensive database for malaria-associated rhythmic transcripts, proteins, and metabolites
authors: Rankawat, S.; Kundal, K.; Singh, S.; Das, S.; Parisi, B.; Korra, B. T.; Rijo-Ferreira, F.; Kumar, R.; Ray, S.
abstract: Abstract: Motivation: The malaria transmission cycle is temporally organized across three interacting biological systems: the parasite, vertebrate host, and mosquito vector. Rhythms in parasite development, host physiology, and vector behavior govern infection dynamics, transmission, and the efficacy of stage-specific antimalarial interventions. However, the molecular architecture connecting these rhythms remains difficult to interrogate because time-resolved omics datasets are distributed across species, experimental paradigms, and analytical frameworks, with no unified resource for comparative analysis. Results: We developed PlasmoRhythm, a curated database integrating 67 transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic datasets from 15 studies, encompassing 1,126 sampling events across Plasmodium species, mammalian hosts, and Anopheles vectors. Harmonized metadata and rhythmicity outputs from JTK_CYCLE, ARSER, Lomb-Scargle, and the meta2d function support interactive cross-study interrogation of molecular profiles. Dedicated modules enable the exploration of rhythmic virulence factors and antimalarial drug interactors, providing a unified framework for hypothesis generation across the malaria transmission cycle. Availability: PlasmoRhythm is freely accessible at https://project.iith.ac.in/cgntlab/PlasmoRhythm/.

title: DNA-Encoded Library-Guided Discovery of a First-in-Class Molecular Glue of the NOS1AP-SCRIB Complex in Alzheimer's Disease Patient-Derived Neurons
authors: Kaur, B.; Abdo, A.; Cho, S.; Gabr, M.
abstract: NOS1AP is an adaptor for neuronal nitric oxide synthase that engages several partner proteins and is implicated in Alzheimer's disease. Efforts to drug NOS1AP have sought to disrupt these; we instead report pharmacological stabilization of one interaction. Affinity selection of a 1.4-billion-member DNA-encoded library identified a benzimidazole-5-carboxamide chemotype, optimized by fragment-directed SAR to NOSTRA with submicromolar NOS1AP binding affinity. Of six interactions, NOSTRA enhanced only SCRIB binding, with a cooperativity factor of 30, predominantly through a 14-fold slowing of dissociation; native mass spectrometry resolved a NOS1AP:NOSTRA:SCRIB ternary complex. In healthy human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, NOSTRA engaged the endogenous complex and activated Rac1 without cytotoxicity; in Alzheimer's patient-derived neurons, it lowered the A{beta}42/A{beta}40 ratio and p-tau217, reduced neurofilament light and improved network activity. With an in vitro ADME profile consistent with CNS exposure, NOSTRA is the first molecular glue for a NOS1AP complex, establishing interaction stabilization as a viable NOS1AP pharmacology.

title: Temporal tuning of actin nucleation by the repurposed DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 encodes distinct axon guidance decisions
authors: Zerkoune, S.; Zagar, Y.; Delaroche, J.; Danicka, J.; Vougny, J.; Uthayasuthan, S.; Aureille, J.; Roche, F.; Haantjes, R.; Gomez-Bravo, C.; Baudet, S.; Denarier, E.; Zainu, A.; Bun, P.; Guillonneau, X.; Debant, A.; Baudat, F.; Nicol, X.; Pietrancosta, N.; Boudeau, J.; Andrieux, A.; Arnal, I.; Antkowiak, A.; Fassier, C.
abstract: Axon guidance is essential for neural circuit assembly and function. While much of the repertoire of guidance cues and receptors is known, its limited diversity cannot fully explain the remarkable complexity of the brain connectome. How temporally ordered, context-dependent intrinsic programs shape the diversity of axonal responses to guidance signals remains poorly understood. We reveal how non-canonical Wnt5a signalling repurposes the DNA repair complex RAD51/fignl1 as a downstream integrator to control retinal ganglion cell axon decision-making at the midline. We demonstrate that differential RAD51/fignl1 expression and interaction dynamics between ipsilateral and contralateral axons tunes the magnitude and temporal dynamics of F-actin nucleation, thereby encoding their trajectory choice. Our findings establish temporal control of cytoskeletal dynamics as a key determinant of axon decision-making and thereby a fundamental layer of circuit wiring. They provide a potential mechanistic framework linking mutations in the DNA repair gene RAD51 to neurodevelopmental disorders with midline guidance defects.

title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
authors: Gutierrez-Jimenez, E.; Wied, B.; Lindhardt, T. B.; Mikkelsen, S. H.; Knopper, R. W.; Skoven, C. S.; Christensen, O. B.; Dashkovskyi, V.; Mrotek, F.; Rasmussen, P. M.; Andresen, M. H.; Krmpot, A.; Khatib, M. E.; Vinogradov, S. A.; Sakadzic, S.; Jensen, M. F.; Pedroza-Pacheco, I.; Postnov, D. D.; Lin, L.; Just, J.; Hansen, B.; Ostergaard, L.
abstract: Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

title: Diurnal Variations in the Cholinergic System of the Nucleus Accumbens
authors: Stowe, T. A.; Huang, Y.; Ferris, M.; McClung, C. A.
abstract: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) plays a critical role in reward-related behaviors, which exhibit diurnal variations. Cholinergic interneurons (CINs) are the primary source of acetylcholine within the NAc and regulate local dopamine (DA) signaling through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Although there are diurnal variations in NAc dynamics, little is known about whether CIN activity and nicotinic signaling also vary across the light/dark cycle. Here, we aimed to determine diurnal variations in the NAc cholinergic system using ex vivo fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and cell-attached electrophysiological recordings in male rodents. We examined time-of-day-dependent differences in nAChR-mediated modulation of DA release, spontaneous CIN firing frequency, and firing patterns. We found that spontaneous CIN firing varied across the light/dark cycle, with increased activity during the dark cycle. Additionally, bath application of nicotine (NIC), mecamylamine (MEC), and dihydro-{beta}-erythroidine (DH{beta}E) reduced CIN firing frequency during the dark cycle, with only MEC decreasing firing frequency in the light cycle. NIC and MEC also altered CIN firing patterns during the dark cycle, whereas DH{beta}E primarily affected firing frequency. Together, these findings demonstrate diurnal variations in NAc CIN activity and reveal time-of-day-dependent differences in the effects of nAChR modulation on spontaneous firing. These results suggest that nicotinic signaling may contribute to diurnal regulation of NAc cholinergic activity, providing insight into mechanisms underlying time-of-day-dependent changes in reward circuitry.
